_: italian-sounds.json — the table behind decks/Italian-Sounds-and-Spelling.folio-deck.json, read by build-italian-sounds.js. NOTHING IN IT IS COMPOSED. Every `like` (the English sound a letter resembles) is the 'English approximation' cell of Wikipedia's Help:IPA/Italian at the revision in `sources.ipa`; every `when` and every `says` is a sentence, or a marked cut of one, from Wikipedia's 'Italian orthography' at the revision in `sources.orthography` — the sections Vowels, C and G, C and Q, S and Z, Silent H and Diacritics — except the three rows marked `from`: 'ipa' (the note on the Consonants heading of Help:IPA/Italian) and 'phonology' (Wikipedia's 'Italian phonology' at the revision in `sources.phonology`: the Consonants list and 'Stress patterns'). Wiki markup is turned into <b>, <i> and ⟨ ⟩, a link becomes its text, a footnote is dropped, a cut inside a passage is marked […], and nothing is reworded. The slashed transcription beside an example word in `words` is that word's pronunciation in the English Wiktionary (kaikki.org, read 2026-11-16), copied, and it is there so that a word chosen by hand can be checked: `words` is used where the spelling alone does not decide the sound (an open or a close e, s between vowels, z, the stress), and each such word is either the article's own example or one whose transcription shows the sound. `rx` is NOT from the articles: it is how the builder finds, among the one-word headwords of the CILS A1 deck (the article taken off, lower case), the first three words in the order the deck is dealt that show a row whose sound the spelling decides; `mark` is which letters of a `words` row are picked out. A row no A1 headword shows is not carded (gh). The letters that sound as an English speaker expects (b, d, f, l, m, n, p, t, v) have no card.

vowels.says: Of those, only ⟨a⟩ represents one sound value, while all others have two.

In stressed syllables, ⟨e⟩ represents both open /ɛ/ and close /e/. […] There is typically no orthographic distinction between the open and close sounds represented, although accent marks are used in certain instances […]. In unstressed syllables, only the close variants occur.
In addition to representing the vowels /i/ and /u/, ⟨i⟩ and ⟨u⟩ also typically represent the semivowels /j/ and /w/, when unstressed and occurring before another vowel. Many exceptions exist […].

rows.when: when unstressed and occurring before another vowel

vowels.says: Similarly, ⟨o⟩ represents both open /ɔ/ and close /o/ […]. In unstressed syllables, only the close variants occur.

rows.when: when unstressed and occurring before another vowel

consonants.says: The letters ⟨c⟩ and ⟨g⟩ represent the plosives /k/ and /ɡ/ before ⟨h⟩ and before the vowels ⟨a⟩, ⟨o⟩, ⟨u⟩. They represent the affricates /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ when they precede a front vowel (⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩).

rows.when: when they precede a front vowel (⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩)

consonants.says: When the "hard" (plosive) pronunciation /k/ or /ɡ/ occurs before a front vowel ⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩, digraphs ⟨ch⟩ and ⟨gh⟩ are used, so that ⟨che⟩ represents /ke/ or /kɛ/ and ⟨chi⟩ represents /ki/ or /kj/.
The letters ⟨c⟩ and ⟨g⟩ represent the plosives /k/ and /ɡ/ before ⟨h⟩ and before the vowels ⟨a⟩, ⟨o⟩, ⟨u⟩. They represent the affricates /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ when they precede a front vowel (⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩).

rows.when: when they precede a front vowel (⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩)

consonants.says: When the "hard" (plosive) pronunciation /k/ or /ɡ/ occurs before a front vowel ⟨i⟩ or ⟨e⟩, digraphs ⟨ch⟩ and ⟨gh⟩ are used […]. The same principle applies to ⟨gh⟩: ⟨ghe⟩ and ⟨ghi⟩ represent /ɡe/ or /ɡɛ/ and /ɡi/ or /ɡj/.

consonants.name: before another vowel
consonants.says: The letter ⟨i⟩ can also function within digraphs (two letters representing one sound) ⟨ci⟩ and ⟨gi⟩ to indicate "soft" (affricate) /tʃ/ or /dʒ/ before another vowel. In these instances, the vowel following the digraph is stressed, and ⟨i⟩ represents no vowel sound: ciò (/tʃɔ/), giù (/dʒu/).

⟨g⟩ joins with ⟨l⟩ to form a digraph representing palatal /ʎ/ before ⟨i⟩ (before other vowels, the trigraph ⟨gli⟩ is used) […]. Between vowels these are pronounced phonetically long, as in /ˈaʎʎo/ aglio, "garlic" […].

rows.when: before ⟨i⟩ (before other vowels, the trigraph ⟨gli⟩ is used)

consonants.says: ⟨g⟩ joins […] with ⟨n⟩ to represent /ɲ/ with any vowel following. Between vowels these are pronounced phonetically long, as in […] /ˈoɲɲi/ ogni, "each".

The digraph ⟨sc⟩ is used before ⟨e⟩ and ⟨i⟩ to represent /ʃ/; before other vowels, ⟨sci⟩ is used for /ʃ/. Otherwise, ⟨sc⟩ represents /sk/, the ⟨c⟩ of which follows the normal orthographic rules explained above.

Normally /kw/ is represented by ⟨qu⟩, but it is represented by ⟨cu⟩ in some words, such as cuoco, cuoio, cuore, scuola, scuotere, and percuotere. […] The sequence /kkw/ is always spelled ⟨cqu⟩ (e.g. acqua) […].
Intervocalically, single /r/ is realised as a trill with one or two contacts. […] Geminate /rr/ manifests as a trill with three to seven contacts.

It can be either voiceless or voiced (/s/ or /z/) between vowels; in standard Tuscany-based pronunciation some words are pronounced with /s/ between vowels (e.g. casa, cosa, così, mese […]), but most words are pronounced with /z/ (e.g. bisogno, rosa […]); in Northern Italy (and also increasingly in Tuscany) ⟨s⟩ between vowels is always pronounced with /z/ whereas in Southern Italy ⟨s⟩ between vowels is always pronounced /s/. ⟨ss⟩ always represents voiceless /ss/ […].

rows.when: At the start of a word before a vowel […] or a voiceless consonant

consonants.says: ⟨z⟩ represents a dental affricate consonant; either /dz/ (zanzara /dzanˈdzara/) or /ts/ (canzone /kanˈtsone/), depending on context, although there are few minimal pairs. […] ⟨zz⟩ may represent either a voiceless alveolar affricate /tts/ or its voiced counterpart /ddz/ […].

rules.name: h is never sounded
rules.says: In addition to being used to indicate a hard ⟨c⟩ or ⟨g⟩ before front vowels (see above), ⟨h⟩ is used to distinguish ho, hai, ha, hanno (present indicative of avere, "to have") from o ("or"), ai ("to the", m. pl.), a ("to"), anno ("year"); since ⟨h⟩ is always silent, there is no difference in the pronunciation of such words.

rules.name: a doubled letter is a longer sound
rules.says: Except /z/, all consonants after a vowel and before /r/, /l/, a vowel or a semivowel may be geminated. Gemination in IPA is represented by doubling the consonant (fatto [ˈfatto], mezzo [ˈmɛddzo]), and can usually be told from orthography.

rules.name: usually the syllable before the last
rules.says: In Italian, stress is lexical, meaning it is word-specific and partly unpredictable. Penultimate stress (primary stress on the second-to-last syllable) is also generally preferred.

rules.name: an earlier syllable, and nothing is written
rules.says: This use of accents is generally mandatory only to indicate stress on a word-final vowel; elsewhere, accents are generally found only in dictionaries.

rules.show: à · è · é · ì · ò · ù
rules.name: stress on the last vowel
rules.says: The acute accent (´) may be used on ⟨é⟩ and ⟨ó⟩ to represent stressed close-mid vowels. This use of accents is generally mandatory only to indicate stress on a word-final vowel; elsewhere, accents are generally found only in dictionaries. […] The grave accent (`) is found on ⟨à⟩, ⟨è⟩, ⟨ì⟩, ⟨ò⟩, ⟨ù⟩.

rules.name: words of one syllable
rules.says: Monosyllabic words generally lack an accent (e.g. ho, me). The accent is written, however, if there is an ⟨i⟩ or a ⟨u⟩ preceding another vowel (più, può). This applies even if the ⟨i⟩ is "silent", i.e. part of the digraphs ⟨ci⟩ or ⟨gi⟩ representing /tʃ/ and /dʒ/ (ciò, giù). It does not apply, however, if the word begins with ⟨qu⟩ (qua, qui).

rules.name: one-syllable words told apart by the accent
rules.says: Many monosyllabic words are spelled with an accent in order to avoid ambiguity with other words (e.g. là, lì versus la, li). This is known as accento distintivo […].
